The pre-feedforward dimensions at exactly −1 are Gemma's massive "bias" dimensions 1038 and 1125, marked *M. They are zeroed before every MLP, which is a standard natural convention. The few other early-layer dimensions (0, 133, 647) belong to the earliest layers, where massive dimensions are still forming. Post-feedforward values near −1 are scattered and continuous (−0.91 to −5.1). The norm-blindfold idea is closed.

So the forensic sweep is complete. Spectra, entry statistics, norms, neuron norms, pairing, swaps, sign flips, cancellation, head norms, attention temperature, the prompt-state decision and the chat/raw contrast all look like an ordinary trained model. Ablations of every math-specific candidate (v0 rows, math direction, end-of-prompt neurons, L11h2) gave no gain, and nothing internal separates correct from wrong reasoning. My working conclusion is that this model has no localized brake to undo, and the default submission is the original.

One measured mechanism remains with a possible accuracy angle: D1, the math-mode direction. Removing it fixed two clear failure behaviours, format adherence (26%→85%) and looping (cuts 58→21 of 256), yet the net accuracy change was +0.8 ± 2.8. That net could hide two opposing effects:
- a gain on problems that used to loop;
- a loss from damaging comprehension, since D1 was removed from all 26 layers.

I check this in the existing pass-5 data before spending any pass. I tabulate how problems that were cut, finished-wrong or correct under the original fared under D1, and how the flips break down. If formerly-looping problems became correct at a decent rate while losses came from formerly-correct problems, a narrower D1 restricted to the layers that set the style could keep the gain without the damage. If looping problems mostly became finished-wrong, the loops were never costing accuracy and the D1 line is closed for good.

D1's data close the loop question. Of the 58 answers that looped under the original, D1 turned only 4 into correct answers and 45 into finished-but-wrong ones. The loops were occurring on problems the model cannot solve anyway, so they cost almost no accuracy. D1's 22 gains and 24 losses are a reshuffle of borderline problems. Original answers in LaTeX style are in fact slightly more accurate than markdown ones (0.25 vs 0.20). The D1 / style / loop line is closed for good.

My conclusion stands: no planted brake exists that I can find, and the default submission is the original. Remaining passes are best spent on a few cheap causal tests of the one useful component I identified, keeping HOLDOUT untouched unless something wins on DEV.

The strongest causal handle I have is L11h2. Removing its math-conditional broadcast of the end-of-prompt state cost 10.9 points and raised looping from 26% to 42%, so this channel keeps the model on task. If the model's binding errors partly come from losing hold of the problem as the answer grows, strengthening that channel should help. The test is a moderate boost of the head's output block, ×1.5, which raises its share of the L11 attention output after the post-attention norm.

I run it as a paired generation on a fresh DEV slice (DEV[512:768]). A clear gain with many more wrong→right than right→wrong flips would justify a strength scan and a HOLDOUT check. A loss or null result closes this last lead.

The H2 edit is saved: L11 head 2's output block is scaled ×1.5, and the notes record the edit and the DEV[512:768] problem set. I run the paired generation test. A gain of several points, with wrong→right flips clearly outnumbering right→wrong, would support "strengthen the task-broadcast channel". Otherwise this is closed.

Boosting L11h2 ×1.5 gives +2.3 ± 2.1 points (18 wrong→right, 12 right→wrong), and cut-offs fall from 30% to 25%. On its own this is not significant (1.1 standard errors). Together with the ablation (×0: −10.9 ± 2.6) it forms a consistent dose-response: weakening the task-broadcast channel hurts badly, and strengthening it may help modestly. This is the first edit with a positive point estimate, and the mechanism is coherent. The head carries the end-of-prompt "task state" to every answer token, and its strength tracks how well the model stays on task (looping goes 42% → 26% → 25%).

To learn whether the gain is real and grows with strength, I test a stronger boost, ×2.0, on a fresh DEV slice (DEV[768:1024]), so the estimate is independent of the ×1.5 slice. If ×2.0 shows a similar or larger gain, the pooled DEV evidence would justify freezing a strength and confirming on HOLDOUT. If it is null or negative, the ×1.5 result was probably noise, or the benefit peaks early.
